source.title: Refusal Behavior in Large Language Models: A Nonlinear Perspective
source.authors: Fabian Hildebrandt; Andreas K. Maier; Patrick Krauss; Achim Schilling

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper’s own activation-analysis results explicitly challenge the claim that refusal is represented by a single linear direction, though they do not test superposition in toy networks or directly establish the dimensionality of individual features.
record.gate_note: The study compares harmful/harmless activation separability after PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP, reporting GDV values and selected layers. It does not test toy-model superposition, feature sparsity or importance, SAE recovery, or whether features are distributed across neurons. The cited results from other work are not recorded as rows. The paper also reports that the smaller Llama model has more mixed embeddings; recorded under fits_no_version because this is not a direct test of the listed LLM feature-spread or SAE claims.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version of the claim. Its rows are GDV separability scores for harmful vs harmless prompts in 2-D PCA, t-SNE and UMAP projections. That measures how well input classes cluster, not whether a feature is a 1-D direction or multi-dimensional. t-SNE and UMAP optimise local cluster structure, so lower GDV than a 2-component PCA does not show nonlinearity. PCA here also captures top-variance axes, not the difference-in-means direction. Superposition is only invoked qualitatively, and no feature dimensionality, neuron spread or SAE recovery is measured. The paper's 'nonlinear refusal' argument concerns a related construct, so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that refusal-related separation is present in all six models with family- and layer-specific patterns: Qwen early, Bloom intermediate, Llama deeper. They argue, against Arditi et al., that refusal is nonlinear and multidimensional rather than a single linear direction, because t-SNE and UMAP give better GDV than PCA.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means activation extraction followed by PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, and GDV analysis on instruction-tuned LLMs; it does not reproduce toy-network feature learning or directly test superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: Separability differs by dimensionality-reduction method, model family, and layer. The selected best-separability layers vary across models and methods.

fits_no_version.finding: t-SNE and UMAP projections give lower (better) harmful/harmless GDV than 2-D PCA in all six models. The authors read this as refusal being nonlinear and multidimensional.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful vs harmless prompt activations cluster more separably under nonlinear 2-D embeddings than under 2-component PCA.

fits_no_version.finding: Llama-3.2-1B shows more mixed harmful/harmless embeddings than Llama-3.2-3B. The authors call this consistent with superposition (qualitative only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A smaller hidden dimension goes with less separable refusal-relevant representations.

fits_no_version.finding: UMAP shows sub-clusters within harmful prompts (Qwen2-1.5B, layer 11) and within harmless prompts (Bloom). This is qualitative, from Fig. 3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful-instruction activations contain sub-clusters suggestive of finer sub-features.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Joint Conference on Neural Network
record.problems: The study infers representational structure from dimensionality-reduced activation visualizations and GDV rather than directly measuring the dimensionality of individual features or testing superposition. It does not report behavioral refusal rates, causal feature interventions, or control comparisons. Table II reports selected lowest-GDV layers rather than a complete numeric set of layerwise results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Figure 4 and the text describe layerwise trends, but the numeric layerwise figure values are not reported in extractable text and are not added as separate rows; the selected-layer GDV results are recorded in Table II rows r1–r18.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity or geometry.
No capacity or importance analysis of neurons.
No analysis of the causes of polysemanticity.
No measure of neuron-level spread and no SAEs.
No measurement of the dimensionality of any feature. The claim that refusal is nonlinear rests on comparing visualisation-method clustering.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all 18 Table II rows to V6 and labelled them challenges/limits_scope. That is not warranted. Comparing GDV across 2-D PCA, t-SNE and UMAP measures how well a visualisation clusters, not the dimensionality of a feature. Table II values are also selected best layers, and the paper does not test the claimed single direction (the difference-in-means vector) itself. The study is therefore relation=discusses, T6, with no verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, sparse features outnumbering dimensions, feature overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons result from limited representational capacity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The study does not measure whether features are spread across neurons or whether an SAE recovers sparse features.
The study does not use or evaluate SAE features as complete, stable, canonical units.

It tests the linear-versus-nonlinear character of refusal-related activation separation, not whether individual superposed features are one-dimensional directions or directly how many dimensions each feature occupies.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: t-SNE and UMAP results across all six tested models
reader_labels.reason: Both nonlinear methods have more negative GDV values than PCA for each model, and the authors conclude that refusal representations are not confined to a simple one-dimensional linear subspace (r2–r3, r5–r6, r8–r9, r11–r12, r14–r15, r17–r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: PCA results across all six tested models
reader_labels.reason: PCA also separates harmful from harmless activations, so the results do not show that linear structure is absent; it is less separative than the nonlinear methods in the reported comparisons (r1, r4, r7, r10, r13, r16).
